engineering.note: Engineering is technical-first, but communication, design context and real-world constraints matter.

computing.note: Computing rewards technical depth; human context, product thinking and ethics become more useful when tied to actual systems.

natural.note: Natural sciences are foundation-heavy; interdisciplinary evidence is secondary unless the intended field is applied.

life.note: Life-science profiles benefit from scientific depth plus credible human, health or social context.

business.note: Business combines quantitative reasoning with communication, markets, organizations and execution.

social.note: Social science is inherently interdisciplinary: strong writing and social analysis are primary, while quantitative evidence can differentiate.

humanities.note: Humanities require sustained reading/writing/interpretation; quantitative or technical work matters only when intellectually integrated.

arts.note: Arts profiles are output-led; interdisciplinary strength comes from a coherent connection between craft, ideas and audience/context.

agriculture.note: Agriculture connects biology and chemistry with environmental systems, food, communities and applied design.

other.note: Interdisciplinary value depends on whether the evidence forms one coherent problem-solving direction.

materials_engineering.note: Materials science sits between physics, chemistry and engineering. Sustainability, computation and design strengthen the profile when they are connected to material behavior or use.

environmental_engineering.note: Environmental engineering is unusually interdisciplinary: chemistry/biology/engineering must connect to systems, sustainability, communities, policy or implementation.

mechanical_engineering.note: Mechanical engineering is physics/design-heavy; interdisciplinary evidence is strongest when attached to devices, users, energy or manufacturing.

chemical_engineering.note: Chemical engineering requires chemistry plus quantitative process thinking; environment/health applications can add coherent breadth.

bioengineering.note: Bioengineering rewards evidence that connects biological systems, engineering design and real human/clinical problems.

biomedical_engineering.note: Biomedical engineering is strongest when technical work is tied to health, users, measurement and ethical/human context.

civil_engineering.note: Civil engineering combines mechanics/materials with infrastructure, environment and public constraints.

energy_engineering.note: Energy work becomes more credible when technical systems are connected to sustainability, economics or deployment constraints.

electrical_engineering.note: Electrical engineering is math/physics/computation intensive; human-context evidence matters when tied to devices or systems.

computer_science.note: CS requires real computational evidence. Interdisciplinary breadth is valuable only when it changes what is built, studied or understood.

artificial_intelligence.note: AI needs math/computation plus evidence of responsible or domain-grounded use; generic AI branding alone is weak evidence.

economics.note: Economics blends quantitative reasoning with causal/social analysis and clear writing.

political_science.note: Political science rewards evidence of institutions, policy, communities and argument; quantitative methods can add depth.

ppe.note: PPE is explicitly cross-disciplinary: philosophy/argument, politics/institutions and economics/quantitative reasoning should connect.

science_technology_society.note: STS requires a genuine bridge between technical systems and their social, historical or ethical consequences.

environmental_studies.note: Environmental studies is systems-oriented and should connect science with policy, society or implementation.

sustainability.note: Sustainability is explicitly interdisciplinary; disconnected technical and social activities should not receive the same credit as integrated work.
